column3: Laser lab. An optical bench seen from above in a hazy dark room: laser beams bounce between small mirrors on rotating mounts, and the beam path itself traces the time (each digit one continuous beam folded by mirrors). Haze makes the beams visible with glow and speckle; mirrors glint where the beam hits; a prism splits white light into a spectrum. Constant life: dust drifting through the beams, slight beam shimmer, a scanning galvo dot. Minute turn: the mirrors of the changing digit rotate on their mounts (eased, physical) and the beam sweeps continuously into its new path, never cut. Hour: the beam routes through the prism and the face becomes a spectral light show, then re-converges. Additive coloured light on black is what this panel does best.

Snow globe. A glass globe fills the square (specular highlight, rim, a wooden base at the bottom), a tiny winter scene inside: a cabin with a warm window, pines, maybe the owner's rainbow frog in a scarf. The time is written in snow: drifts on the ground or snow resting on shapes. Snow keeps falling gently all the time. Minute turn: an invisible hand gives the globe a little shake: the globe wobbles, flakes whirl up from the changed digit, swirl in a curl-noise vortex and settle into the new digit. Hour: a big shake, a blizzard, and the aurora inside the glass, with the time readable throughout. Physical particles, settling, glass refraction at the rim.

The frog painter. The owner's avatar, a rainbow frog in round glasses, big and expressive (20+ px), stands at an easel and paints the time on its canvas with a brush; a palette of paint blobs in its other hand. Brush-stroke letterforms: visible bristle texture, wet paint sheen, the colour of the paint on the brush. Rest: the frog breathes, blinks, pushes up its glasses, catches a fly with its tongue, taps its brush. Minute turn: the frog paints over the changing digit and paints the new one stroke by stroke in stroke order (blank or partial is fine, a different number is not). Hour: the frog steps back, admires, signs the canvas, and swaps in a fresh canvas painted in a new colour scheme. Charm and animation craft are the point.

Vector arcade. A colour vector monitor from 1979 (Asteroids, Tempest): glowing lines with phosphor persistence, bloom and a slight beam wobble, on pure black. The digits are big vector rocks shaped as numerals, tumbling slowly in place (a few degrees, always readable). A little ship drifts, thrusts, rotates and fires all the time. Minute turn: the ship shoots the changing digit; it bursts into its own line segments, which fly apart and spin, then drift back and reassemble into the new digit (the same segments: physical continuity). Hour: a UFO crosses with its warble, a chain of explosions, and the ship does a victory loop. Line drawing with sub-pixel anti-aliasing is essential.

Ink in water. A real-time fluid (stable fluids on a 64x64 grid is cheap): coloured inks bloom and curl like ink dropped into a glass of water. The digits are drawn by ink: drops fall in from above and spread into plumes that hold the digit shape, constantly refed so they stay readable, with tendrils and Kelvin-Helmholtz curls at their edges. Minute turn: a vortex stirs the old digit away and new drops fall in along the new shape. Hour: a big swirl marbles all the colours together like Ebru, then the time re-forms. Keep it deterministic: warmup <= 2 s, so design the sim to forget its past fast (or derive state from the minute).

Metro map. The time drawn as a transit diagram, Harry Beck / Vignelli style: each digit is one coloured line with 45-degree bends and rounded corners, stations as white ticks, interchanges as rings where lines meet, a river in pale blue. The square grid is native to 0/45/90-degree lines. Trains (bright dots with short tails) glide along every line all the time, stopping at stations. Minute turn: the changing digit's line closes (trains leave, it fades to a dashed 'under construction' line) and a track-laying train draws the new route. Hour: night service: the map dims to night colours and a single night bus traces every line, or a new line opens with a ribbon. Graphic, crisp, alive.

Pinball. A pinball table seen from above fills the panel: flippers at the bottom, pop bumpers that flash, slingshots, lane guides, a ramp, chrome rails. A silver ball (specular glint, real physics: gravity down the slope, bounces) is always in play, and the flippers react to it. The time is the table's own light show: the playfield's lit inserts (arrows, stars, round lamps) are arranged as digits and glow under the plastic. Minute turn: the ball hits the drop-target bank of the changing digit, targets drop, lamps chase, and the new digit lights insert by insert. Hour: multiball, everything flashes, a DMD-style JACKPOT. A game the owner would want to watch.

Paper-cut shadow box. Five or six layers of cut paper (kirigami lightbox): mountains, a forest, a fox or frog, clouds, each layer a flat silhouette in its own tone, backlit by a sky gradient that follows the time of day (dawn pinks, noon blue, dusk orange, night with stars and moon). The time is cut into one paper layer as stencil letterforms (with the bridges real paper cutting needs). The view drifts slowly so the layers parallax; edges catch light. Minute turn: the changing digit's paper piece hinges up and folds away like a pop-up book and the new one unfolds into place. Hour: a whole pop-up page turn, layers sliding in from the sides.

Sandcastle beach. A wide 128x64 side view: sky (sun or moon placed by the time of day), the sea on one side with rolling, breaking waves and foam, a beach of textured sand. The digits are sandcastles: towers, crenellations, little flags, windows, moats; sandcastle letterforms. A crab (a character, 6+ px) scuttles, waves its claws, rebuilds; gulls glide. Minute turn: a wave rolls in over the changing digit, slumps it into wet, darker sand that flows and settles (sand physics), the wave retreats, and the crab builds the new digit with bucket-shaped towers popping out. Hour: a big tide washes all four, and they are rebuilt with fanfare.

Marble machine. A tall 64x128 Rube Goldberg marble run: zigzag rails, a lift wheel or screw lift carrying marbles up one side, a spinning wheel, a bell that rings, glossy glass marbles in colours with specular highlights rolling with real physics along the tracks. The time is shown by marbles held in glass tubes shaped like the digits (stacked marbles). Minute turn: the changing digit's gate opens, its marbles drop out and run through the machine, and the new digit's tube fills from a hopper (partly filled must never read as a different number). Hour: every marble cascades through the whole machine, then refills. Satisfying, mechanical, endless motion.

Voxel city. A 128x128 isometric diorama: a tiny island town built of voxels (cubes with three shaded faces), water with shimmer around it, trees, little cars and boats moving, windows that light up at night, day and night lighting from the clock. The digits are voxel buildings or block towers standing on the island. Minute turn: the changing digit's blocks are dismantled by a crane (or hop off) and fly in arcs to stack into the new digit, Tetris-like but physical. Hour: the whole island rotates 90 degrees in isometric 3D (real re-projection, smooth), revealing the time again from the new side, with a hot-air balloon or fireworks. Real 3D shading and shadows.

Lighthouse. The big panel is the night sea, a rocky coast at one edge. The lighthouse lamp itself is the separate 8x8 board beside the panel: a bright rotating Fresnel lens with prism glints, brightest when it faces you. Its beam sweeps across the sea like a radar, lighting haze and the waves, and reveals the time written in the sea (foam, rocks, a fleet of boats, buoys), readable faintly by moonlight between sweeps and brightly in the beam. Minute turn: something physical changes the digit (a boat sails out and another in, fog rolls over it, the tide). Hour: the lamp flashes the hour count in a lighthouse character and the beam makes a slow full-power sweep, perhaps a foghorn ripple. The two boards are two objects in one world.

Sand tile. A single 25 mm 8x8 tile running falling-sand physics: each LED a grain or empty, grains pile, slide and flow. The time is told by sand: it pours in and piles into the hour, then gravity turns (the tile 'tips' virtually: the real board has an IMU, so this is what it would do when you tilt it) and the sand flows into the minutes, and back. Grains glide with sub-pixel motion during flow. Find a way the time reads on 8x8 at true size (two digits at a time, or a non-digit system), with sand colours (warm amber, dusk strata). Keep within the board's heat budget.

Digit pets. Four 8x8 tiles in a row, each a tiny creature whose body IS its digit (numberfolk at 8x8): eyes, a blink, a bob, maybe feet; each digit has a personality and its own colour. They look at each other across the seams, sleep at night (Zzz), wake in the morning. Minute turn: the changing creature hops out of its tile (the seam is a 6 mm gap it must jump), and the new digit creature hops in from the next tile or drops in from above. Hour: all four do a wave or dance and swap places. Each tile runs on its own MCU; they stay in step by the clock.
